newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Polish poet Szymborska wins Nobel literary prize.
newsitem.headline: Polish poet Szymborska wins Nobel literary prize.

text.p: Polish poet and critic Wislawa Szymborska won the 1996 Nobel Literature Prize on Thursday at the age of 73, the Swedish Academy said.

The academy said it was honouring Szymborska, who lives in the southern city of Krakow, for "poetry that with ironic precision allows the historical and biological context to come to light in fragments of human reality".
The award surprised observers, who had expected a novelist to win the $1.12 million award after Irish poet Seamus Heaney won last year's prize.
It also surprised the laureate herself. She told Reuters she was delighted but also apprehensive at being flung into the world literary limelight.

"This is a difficult situation. I am normally a very private person and now I forsee some difficult moments," Szymborska, laughing with excitement, said by telephone from a hotel for writers in the Polish mountain resort of Zakopane.

"Since 1957 -- when censorship had lost its stranglehold after the thaw of the previous year -- she has published a handful of slim but powerful collections of poems, a few volumes of book reviews and a number of highly esteemed translations of earlier French poetry," the academy said in its citation.
It said Szymborska's poetry was very difficult to translate because of its stylistic variety.
"With her distance and commitment, Szymborska accords full support to her idea that no questions are of such significance as those that are naive," the Swedish academicians said.
From 1953 to 1981, Szymborska was on the editorial staff of the Polish intellectual magazine Zycie Literackie (Literary Life).
The academy said a typical example of her work could be found at the end of a poem called "The Joy of Writing".
"The joy of writing.
Power of preserving.
The revenge of a mortal hand."

A selection of 100 of her poems have been translated into English under the title "View with a Grain of Sand." Poems range from "Calling out to Yeti," written in 1957, to "The End and the Beginning" written in 1993.
The Yeti in Szymborska's poems is associated with late Soviet leader Josef Stalin.
"In her discourse there is a striking combination of spirit, inventiveness and empathy, which calls to mind both the Renaissance and the Baroque," the academy said.
Szymborka's German publisher said he was overjoyed by the award, which provoked scenes of jubilation at his Frankfurt book fair stand.

Dr Rainer Weiss, editor-in-chief of Suhrkamp, said the award, that left him facing a bevy of reporters in a state of delighted shock, was sure to give a big boost to sales of the poet's works which Suhrkamp had been publishing since 1973.
Szymborska herself paid warm tribute on Thursday to Anders Bodegard, Swedish translator of her poems.
"If this had been a mediocre translator we would not be talking today," she said.
Szymborska is the fourth Pole to win the literature prize.

Henryk Sienkiewicz won it in 1905, only the sixth winner of the prize bequeathed by dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, Wladyslaw Reymont won in 1924 -- when he shared the prize with Briton George Bernard Shaw -- and Polish-born American Czeslaw Milosz won in 1980.
